title: Silky Rice Congee with Ginger, Crispy Shallots and Spring Onion
summary: A gently simmered, silky rice porridge enriched with ginger and finished with crisp fried shallots, spring onion and a savoury drizzle of soy and sesame oil.
equipment: large heavy saucepan or casserole (at least 4 litres) with a lid

ingredients.item: jasmine or other long-grain white rice
low-salt chicken stock or vegetable stock
water, plus up to 250 ml more
fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thick slices
ingredients.note: removed before serving; counted in full

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Rinse the rice
steps.text: Rinse the rice in a sieve under cold running water until the water runs almost clear. This clears away loose surface starch that would otherwise make the congee gluey rather than smoothly creamy once the grains break down.

steps.title: Bring everything to a boil
steps.text: Put the rinsed rice, stock, 1.5 litres water, ginger slices and salt into the large pan and bring to a boil over high heat, stirring now and then so nothing catches on the base. Starting the rice in a flavoured liquid means the grains absorb seasoning as they cook, rather than trying to season a finished porridge afterwards.

steps.title: Simmer low and slow
steps.text: Turn the heat down to a steady gentle simmer, rest the lid ajar (a wooden spoon laid across the pan under the lid stops it boiling over) and cook for 60-75 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes and scraping the base. It's ready when the grains have broken down into a thick, glossy, creamy porridge; add up to 250 ml more water along the way if it gets thicker than a loose porridge. The long, gentle simmer ruptures the rice grains so their starch spills into the liquid, which is what gives congee its characteristic silky thickness. Fish out the ginger slices once it's done.

steps.title: Fry the crispy shallots
steps.text: While the congee simmers, put the sliced shallots and oil into a cold frying pan, set it over medium heat and cook, stirring, for 5-8 minutes until evenly golden and crisp; they colour quickly in the last minute, so watch closely. Lift onto kitchen paper with a slotted spoon and keep the flavoured oil. Starting them in cold oil lets the moisture inside the shallots evaporate gradually, so they crisp through evenly instead of browning outside while staying soft in the middle.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Ladle the congee into bowls and top with the crispy shallots, a spoonful of the shallot oil, the sliced spring onions, a few drops each of soy sauce and sesame oil, and a pinch of white pepper. Serve straight away while hot, since congee keeps thickening as it sits and the toppings are best added fresh for contrast and crunch.

tips: Common mistake: simmering with the lid fully on. Congee can boil over and scorch on the base if the steam has nowhere to go, so keep the lid propped ajar as described.
Stir every 10 minutes and scrape the base, since the rice settles and can catch on the bottom of the pan during the long simmer.
Loosen leftover congee with a splash of water as you reheat it, since it thickens considerably once chilled.
Fry the shallots in a cold pan rather than a hot one so they crisp through evenly instead of burning on the outside.
Taste and adjust the soy sauce and white pepper at the table, since the base congee itself is only lightly salted.
storage: Congee thickens as it cools; refrigerate within 1 hour and use within 24 hours. Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring, until it's bubbling and piping hot (74°C) before serving. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
